paragraphs: Whenever we discuss the political laws of the United States, we must start with the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people. This principle lies, to a greater or lesser degree, at the bottom of almost all human institutions, yet it usually stays hidden from view. People obey it without recognizing it, or if it is briefly brought into the light, it is hurriedly thrust back into the darkness of the sanctuary. “The will of the nation” is one of the phrases that the crafty and the despotic of every age have abused most shamelessly. Some have pictured it in the purchased votes of a few servants of power; others in the votes of a timid or self-interested minority; and some have even found it in a people’s silence, on the assumption that the mere fact of submission established the right to command.

In America the principle of the sovereignty of the people is neither barren nor hidden, as it is in some other nations. The customs recognize it and the laws proclaim it. It spreads freely and reaches its most remote consequences without obstruction. If there is any country in the world where the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people can be fairly judged, where it can be studied as it is applied to the affairs of society, and where its dangers and its advantages can be foreseen, that country is certainly America.

I have already observed that, from their origin, the sovereignty of the people was the fundamental principle of most of the British colonies in America. But it was far from having then the influence on the government of society that it has now. Two obstacles, one external and one internal, held back its advance. It could not openly show itself in the laws of colonies that were still required to obey the mother country. It was therefore forced to spread in secret and to gain ground in the provincial assemblies, and especially in the townships.

American society was not yet prepared to adopt it with all its consequences. The intelligence of New England and the wealth of the country south of the Hudson (as I showed in the preceding chapter) long exercised a kind of aristocratic influence, which tended to keep the exercise of social authority in the hands of a few. Public officials were not all elected, and not all citizens were voters. The right to vote was everywhere kept within certain limits and made to depend on a certain qualification, which was extremely low in the North and higher in the South.

Then the American Revolution broke out, and the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people, which had been nurtured in the townships and municipalities, took possession of the state. Every class was enlisted in its cause. Battles were fought and victories won for it, until it became the law of laws.
A change just as rapid took place within society itself, where the law of descent completed the destruction of local influences.

At the very time when this consequence of the laws and of the Revolution was plain to every eye, victory was irrevocably declared for the democratic cause. All power was in fact in its hands, and resistance was no longer possible. The higher orders submitted without a murmur and without a struggle to an evil that was now inevitable. The usual fate of falling powers awaited them. Each of their members followed his own interests, and since it was impossible to wrest power from the hands of a people they did not hate enough to defy, their only aim was to win its good will at any price. The most democratic laws were therefore voted by the very men whose interests they harmed. And so, although the higher classes did not stir up the passions of the people against their own order, they hastened the triumph of the new state of things. By a strange reversal, the democratic impulse proved most irresistible in the very States where the aristocracy had the firmest hold. Maryland, which had been founded by men of rank, was the first State to proclaim universal suffrage and to introduce the most democratic forms into the conduct of its government.

When a nation changes the qualification for voting, it is easy to foresee that sooner or later the qualification will be abolished altogether. There is no more constant rule in the history of society: the further voting rights are extended, the greater the need to extend them. After each concession the strength of the democracy grows, and its demands grow with its strength. The ambition of those who fall below the set level is irritated in exact proportion to the number of those who rise above it. The exception finally becomes the rule, concession follows concession, and there is no stopping point short of universal suffrage.

Today the principle of the sovereignty of the people has reached, in the United States, every practical development the imagination can conceive. It is free of the fictions that have been draped over it in other countries, and it appears in every possible form as the occasion requires. Sometimes the people as a body make the laws, as at Athens. Sometimes its representatives, chosen by universal suffrage, transact business in its name and almost under its direct control.

In some countries there is a power that is, to some extent, foreign to the social body, and that directs it and forces it along a certain path. In others the ruling force is divided, lying partly within and partly outside the ranks of the people. But nothing of the kind is to be seen in the United States. There society governs itself for itself. All power is centered in its own bosom, and you will scarcely meet a single individual who would venture to conceive, much less to express, the idea of seeking power elsewhere. The nation takes part in making its laws by choosing its legislators, and in carrying them out by choosing the agents of the executive government. It may almost be said to govern itself, so feeble and so restricted is the share left to the administration, and so little do the authorities forget their popular origin and the power from which they derive. *a [Footnote a: See Appendix, H.]
